question:
We are planning a project that depends on a third-party API nobody on the team has used and on a performance target we may not be able to reach. How should we handle these things that could go wrong, both when planning the work and while it is under way?

Answer with a list of guidelines. After each guideline, cite the source it comes from: the path of the SWEBOK file if you have it, otherwise a verbatim quote of at least 8 words from the passage, in the form (source: ...).
answer:
Excellent results across all four searches. I now have rich, specific SWEBOK passages to build a thorough, cited list of guidelines. Here they are:

---

## Guidelines for Handling the Unfamiliar API and Uncertain Performance Target

The guidelines are organized in two phases: **during planning**, then **while work is under way**.

---

### Phase 1 — During Planning

**1. Understand risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, then build a risk register.**

Distinguish between uncertainty (lack of information — which describes your situation with the new API and unproven performance) and risk (the effect that uncertainty has on objectives). Formally identify, analyse, and prioritize each risk factor, then record all of them in a risk register.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt e2a2cb43fc578e221506]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Risk Management and Quality Assessment/Risk Management_ Identification, Analysis, and Mitigation Strategies.md`)

---

**2. Conduct a feasibility analysis before committing to the work.**

Before locking in scope, schedule, and budget, explicitly examine whether the performance target and the unfamiliar API are achievable within your constraints.

> (source: Feasibility Analysis is listed as a first step under "Initiation and Scope Definition" in the Software Engineering Management chapter: "1.2. Feasibility Analysis"
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Software Requirements Engineering Fundamentals/Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge V4/SWEBOK Guide Version 4.0 Overview/SWEBOK Guide Version 4.0a Table of Contents.md`, swebok-v4_table_11)

---

**3. Use a risk-driven architecture approach: address the most dangerous unknowns first in your architecture.**

Shape the architecture around the identified risks — the unfamiliar API and performance target are exactly the kind of "extremely demanding quality requirements" or "small solution space" scenarios this approach targets.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt c53642a9dd3b515e1f3d]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Architecture_ Foundations, Methods, and Modern Practice/Risk-Driven Software Architecture Approach.md`)

---

**4. At the architectural design stage, explicitly develop strategies to address performance as a crosscutting concern.**

Performance must be a first-class concern at the architecture level, not deferred to construction.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt f133816fdc3291e76ba8]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Software Development Stages and Design Architecture/Software Architecture Design and Computational Models.md`)

---

**5. Build a prototype early to explore the least-understood aspects — especially the third-party API and performance feasibility.**

Prototyping specifically targets the riskiest, least-understood parts first, the opposite of starting with what you already know.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt dd9033f7b0e5f3b3418e]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Engineering Processes and Quality Assurance/Formal Methods, Agile Development, and Software Quality/Verification and Prototyping Approaches/Prototyping Methods in Software Engineering.md`)

---

**6. Treat prototype construction as a planned, monitored activity — not an ad hoc spike.**

A prototype should [SWEBOK excerpt c1aa6b55625e9848dc44], not a free-form experiment.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 3a78a626dbc85c781d54]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Engineering Decision-Making Through Data and Standards/Modeling, Simulation, and Measurement in Engineering/Modeling, Simulation, and Prototyping for System Analysis/Prototyping in Software and Physical Systems.md`)

---

**7. Use simulation or formal design analysis to predict performance before committing to a design.**

Rather than relying entirely on testing later, use formal design analysis or performance simulation to validate performance properties early.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 7c9848044a0924e23933]… [SWEBOK excerpt e9370b60de6cf6bb205e])."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Design Quality Evaluation and Assessment/Design Analysis and Quality Metrics/Formal Analysis and Dynamic Evaluation Techniques.md`)

---

**8. Understand the economics of your performance target — distinguish the "fail point" from the "perfection point" and from the most cost-effective level.**

Performance targets are often arbitrary; understand the economic value curve. Even if the stated target cannot be fully met, the software may still have value. Also identify the minimum performance below which the project is not viable ("fail point").

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 58507504e5c6582e97d8]… [SWEBOK excerpt 71276f5618f7ce9e0752]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Engineering_ Viability, Verification, and Stakeholder Management/Performance Thresholds and Cost-Effective Quality Optimization/Fail Point and Performance Requirements in Software Systems.md`)

---

**9. When planning, incorporate the magnitude of risk into how much planning effort you invest — plan the management of the plan itself.**

The amount of planning effort should be calibrated to the risks involved; do not plan lightly for a risky endeavour. The plan management itself must be planned.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 31428eabea66a8ec8aa2]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Planning, Execution, and Control of Software Projects/Planning and Process Management in Software Projects/Software Project Planning and Change Management.md`)

---

**10. Assess the third-party API for risk, legality, and suitability — and introduce technical or procedural controls for external dependencies.**

Acquiring an external API is a form of software acquisition. Assess it for risk and suitability, and introduce controls to mitigate the exposure it creates.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 184a2ab9d57169b59ee8]… [SWEBOK excerpt e3ca00f82a82d0e84520]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Supplier Contract Management.md`)

---

**11. Manage the third-party API's dependency supply chain: avoid unnecessary dependencies, watch for license conflicts and propagated vulnerabilities.**

Each dependency — including the API and its transitive dependencies — introduces potential risk and must be actively managed.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt dca20a7629ae39fd2e86]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Construction Methods and Languages/Dependency Management and Construction Practices/Managing Software Dependencies and Supply Chain Risks.md`)

---

**12. Regardless of how you acquire or integrate the third-party API, verify and validate it against your architectural design and requirements.**

Do not assume an acquired component works correctly in your context; always verify completeness, correctness, and fitness for purpose in your intended environment.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 9258a9a924333ed00995]… [SWEBOK excerpt 221beed077ae21dfea32]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Supplier Contract Management.md`)

---

### Phase 2 — While the Work Is Under Way

**13. Conduct risk management repeatedly throughout the project life cycle — not just at the start.**

Risk management is not a one-time planning activity. It must recur at regular intervals as the project progresses.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 9796a64f0b7b797d303d]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Risk Management and Quality Assessment/Continuous Risk and Quality Management/Risk Management Throughout Project Life Cycle.md`)

---

**14. Continually monitor the project's risk profile; recalculate risk exposures and act when thresholds are exceeded.**

Track the evolving risk picture throughout execution. When a risk exposure exceeds a predefined threshold, report it and respond.

> (source: "Risk exposures should be recalculated… [SWEBOK excerpt 015b2c96293ad2fc568a]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Project Oversight/Risk Monitoring and Control Management/Risk Exposure Recalculation and Threshold Monitoring.md`)

---

**15. Use ongoing project monitoring — including adherence to scope, schedule, and cost — as the basis for risk-informed decisions.**

Monitoring data drives control decisions. Where [SWEBOK excerpt b8b6e128d8ffb0e3df2f], project changes (corrective actions) can be made.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt b4273c01757398e99d73])."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Project Oversight/Risk Monitoring and Control Management/Project Monitoring and Risk-Based Decision Making.md`)

---

**16. Revisit the project risk profile explicitly during the monitor process, alongside adherence to quality requirements.**

When monitoring each task's outputs, do not treat risk review as optional — it is a mandatory part of the monitoring cycle.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 6d5d3c98e2ff5598bd88]… [SWEBOK excerpt 5288f091eeda229b8dce]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Project Oversight/Data Acquisition and Project Measurement/Implementation and Monitoring of Software Project Measurement.md`)

---

**17. When control actions are taken, document and communicate all decisions, revise plans accordingly, and record all relevant data.**

The control loop is not just about taking action — it requires traceability: document what was decided, tell everyone affected, update the plans, and record the evidence.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 6fa70f6c5d61d4c1ee2a]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Project Oversight/Risk Monitoring and Control Management/Software Project Control and Configuration Management.md`)

---

**18. As a last resort, the control process may lead to project abandonment — this must be a recognized option, agreed with all relevant stakeholders beforehand.**

Deciding in advance under what conditions a project should be stopped is a legitimate and recommended part of risk management.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 6a23fb82ccee3390085f]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Software Acquisition and Project Oversight/Risk Monitoring and Control Management/Software Project Control and Configuration Management.md`; and: "[SWEBOK excerpt e7c5b4403decffed2232]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Risk Management and Quality Assessment/Risk Assessment Methods and Software Project Risk Management.md`)

---

**19. Use profiling and performance analysis tools during construction to detect performance problems early.**

Do not wait for final integration to discover performance shortfalls; use dedicated tooling throughout construction.

> (source: "Profiling, Performance Analysis, and Slicing Tools" is listed as a construction tool category (section 5.4) in the Software Construction chapter.
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Software Requirements Engineering Fundamentals/Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge V4/SWEBOK Guide Version 4.0 Overview/SWEBOK Guide Version 4.0a Table of Contents.md`, swebok-v4_table_5)

---

**20. Conduct periodic performance reviews of project personnel and processes — not just the product — to detect problems with adherence to plans.**

Team and process performance reviews can surface signs of difficulty before they escalate into risk events.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 352063d0445fbc6155fe]… [SWEBOK excerpt ed979a37df0e59fae2e0]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Reviewing and Evaluating Project Performance.md`)

---

**21. Conduct retrospective analysis at the end of phases or iterations; feed lessons back into the project and the organization.**

Each phase or iteration is an opportunity to analyze what risks materialized, what worked, and what did not, so the whole organization learns.

> (source: "[SWEBOK excerpt 238bfc70468a6a5f0b12]… [SWEBOK excerpt 8d1b90f05e370d9ee05c]."
> — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Quality Management and Project Oversight/Software Measurement and Organizational Learning/Software Engineering Measurement and Organizational Learning.md`)
